source: Wikipedia (accessed 2026) Expected value of perfect information
finding: EVPI is the expected payoff with perfect information minus the best expected payoff without it. It is never negative. It is used in health economics (NICE) to price the cost of decision uncertainty.
numbers: EVPI = sum_j p_j max_i R_ij - max_i sum_j p_j R_ij
quote: Since EV|PI is necessarily greater than or equal to EMV, EVPI is always non-negative.
limits: Needs a payoff matrix and priors. A pure upper bound, it says nothing about which real test to run.
agent_relevance: Gives the ceiling for any test. If a test costs more than EVPI, skip all tests (S4/S7).

source: Dong et al. (2026) Value of Information: A Framework for Human-Agent Communication
finding: An LLM agent estimates a belief over user intents, computes the expected utility gain of each candidate question (VoI), subtracts a per-question cost, and asks only if net VoI is above zero. No tuned threshold.
numbers: Four domains: Mixed 20 Questions (animal reward 1, medical reward 10), flight recommendation, ambiguous WebShop, e-commerce. Models GPT-4.1 and Gemini-2.5-Flash. VoI matched or beat the best grid-searched baseline in 18 of 20 conditions. Up to +1.36 utility in high-cost settings.
quote: matches or exceeds the best manually-tuned baselines, achieving up to 1.36 utility points higher in high-cost settings
limits: Belief is elicited from the LLM, whose calibration was only fair (worse for medical). Utilities and costs are set by the designer. Two models only.
agent_relevance: Direct template for S4/S7: ask or act by net VoI, with cost as an explicit input.

source: Dong et al. (2026) VoI vs confidence thresholding, Mixed 20Q
finding: With cost c=0.01 on Mixed 20Q, VoI beat the best tuned confidence-threshold baseline. The threshold baseline needed re-tuning for every task and cost.
numbers: VoI utility 14.14 vs best confidence threshold 11.49 (threshold 0.90). Threshold baseline tuned over 9 values.
limits: Single cost setting quoted. A tuned threshold was comparable on GPT-4 for some tasks (Mixed 20Q, WebShop).
agent_relevance: Confidence alone ignores stakes. Use stake-weighted VoI, not 'ask when unsure'.

source: Dong et al. (2026) Stakes-sensitivity case study
finding: Same cost c=0.05: VoI kept asking in the high-stakes medical case (reward 10) and stopped early in the low-stakes animal case (reward 1). A confidence threshold does the same in both.
numbers: Reward 10 vs 1, cost 0.05. Single qualitative instance; the VoI agent still reached a wrong diagnosis in the shown medical example.
limits: Case study of one instance, not a rate.
agent_relevance: Stopping rule should scale with the payoff of being right.

source: Dong et al. (2026) Baseline comparison: fixed-round and adaptive prompting
finding: Fixed-round questioning has an inverted-U utility curve against number of questions. Asking the LLM whether it feels confident is inconsistent and below structured methods. No-question is near zero accuracy on Mixed 20Q unless cost is very high.
numbers: Qualitative from Figure 2; No-Question accuracy near zero on Mixed 20Q.
limits: Per-method numbers are in figures and appendix tables, not read in full.
agent_relevance: Do not rely on a prompt saying 'ask if needed'. Compute the stop rule in code (G5).

source: Dong et al. (2026) Calibration analysis
finding: The VoI method needs the LLM's belief distribution. Models were reasonably calibrated on animal guessing and less so on medical diagnosis. VoI still held up.
numbers: Argmax-based calibration only; no ground-truth distribution.
limits: Calibration was checked with a weak proxy.
agent_relevance: The weak link in LLM VoI is the belief estimate, so check it with code where possible.

source: Hu et al. (2024) Uncertainty of Thoughts (UoT)
finding: A tree search simulates answers to candidate questions. Reward is information gain over a set of candidate hypotheses, propagated up the tree. The best question is the one with highest expected reward. Tested on 20 Questions, medical diagnosis, troubleshooting.
numbers: Mean success rate gain over direct prompting 38.1 percent across 5 datasets and 5 LLMs. Llama3-70B +46.6. Beats CoT-SC by 33.8 and Reflexion by 29.9. Troubleshooting GPT-4 43.7 to 67.3. DX medical 97.0 percent with GPT-4. MedDG 81.4 (Gemini 1.5 Pro) and 88.0 (GPT-4).
quote: UoT improves the success rate of multiple LLMs by 38.1% on average compared with direct prompting
limits: Simplified closed-set setting: answers must cleanly eliminate candidates. GPT-4 acts as the answerer. Authors note incomplete elimination is not handled.
agent_relevance: Information gain over an explicit candidate set is a usable question selector. This is EIG, a cheaper cousin of VoI.

source: Hu et al. (2024) UoT equal-token comparison (Table 2)
finding: At matched GPT-4 token budget, uncertainty-based reward beats heuristic self-evaluation reward in tree search for question choice.
limits: Token counts measured on GPT-4 only.
agent_relevance: Information-gain reward beat a model's own judgement of a question. Fits G5: code scores, model does not.

source: Hu et al. (2024) UoT reward ablation
finding: Swapping ToT's self-evaluation reward for the uncertainty reward helps by about 5.9 points on average. In 20 Questions, CoT and planning prompting did worse than plain GPT-4.
numbers: ToT with uncertainty reward +5.9 average. UoT open-set +8.7 over Adapted-ToT. UoT closed-set +4.3 over second-best Reflexion.
limits: Averages over 3 tasks.
agent_relevance: Generic reasoning prompts (CoT) do not fix question choice; a purpose-built score does.

source: Hu et al. (2024) UoT significance test
finding: Authors repeated DP vs UoT three times on five datasets with GPT-4 and Llama 3 and ran t-tests. Because of API quota limits the runs were few.
numbers: Three repeats per setting; t-statistics and p-values in appendix Tables 7 and 8.
limits: Only 3 repeats.
agent_relevance: Effect is probably real but the number of runs is small.

source: Li, Kim and Wang (2025) QuestBench
finding: Underspecified reasoning problems framed as constraint satisfaction with exactly one missing variable. The model must pick the one question that resolves it. Models do well on math word problems and poorly on logic and planning.
numbers: Models: GPT-4o, o1-preview, Claude 3.5 Sonnet, Gemini 1.5 Pro/Flash, Gemini 2.0 Flash Thinking, Gemma 2. GSM-Q and GSME-Q above 80 percent. Logic-Q and Planning-Q under 50 percent. CoT and 4-shot gave no significant gain across all models.
quote: all models we tested struggled to perform beyond 50% on our Logic-Q and Planning-Q domains
limits: 1-sufficient problems only. Multiple-choice question set. Models are 2024 vintage; a Gemini 2.5 Pro trace is shown only as an example.
agent_relevance: Choosing which test to run is its own skill, weak even when the model can solve the problem. Add a code step that enumerates candidate tests.

source: Li, Kim and Wang (2025) QuestBench ablation: question vs reasoning
finding: Restricting to items where the model solved the fully specified version did not fix question choice. Knowing how to solve is necessary but not enough for knowing what is missing.
numbers: Logic-Q accuracy unchanged after filtering. Planning-Q slightly up. GSM-Q/GSME-Q change from up 39 points to down about 10 depending on model.
limits: Per-model tables not fully read.
agent_relevance: Question-asking needs a separate check from solving.

source: Li, Kim and Wang (2025) QuestBench: detecting underspecification
finding: Models rarely say 'not sure' on hard planning problems, they guess. The ground-truth share of underspecified items was 41.8 percent but models said 'not sure' almost never.
numbers: Planning-Q zero-shot 'not sure' rate: Gemini Flash Thinking 1.4 percent, Claude 3.5 4.6 percent, GPT-4o 0.7 percent, versus 41.8 percent true. F1 at most 5 points above random in Planning-Q.
limits: Zero-shot, no CoT, 2024 models.
agent_relevance: Models do not know when they lack information. The program must detect it (G1: signals from code).

source: Li, Kim and Wang (2025) QuestBench difficulty axes
finding: In Logic-Q accuracy falls with search depth, variables, constraints and expected brute-force guesses. In Planning-Q there is little correlation, so models are not doing a backward search.
numbers: Spearman correlations significant for most models in Logic-Q; weak or none in Planning-Q.
limits: Correlational.
agent_relevance: Do not trust model-internal search to find the key missing fact; give it a structured list.

source: Park, Im and Kwon (2026) Selective Critique, SAG
finding: A gate decides each step whether to call an expensive critic. It uses action entropy and top-2 margin as a proxy for the value of information of critique. A Bayes-optimal threshold lemma says call the critic only when expected gain exceeds cost.
numbers: ALFWorld 24.6 percent (no critique) to 78.4 with SAG. Average relative gain over ReAct 91 percent across 3 benchmarks x 3 backbones. 3.1x normalized token efficiency. 7B actor plus 3B critic close to 14B actor.
limits: VoI is approximated by uncertainty proxies, not measured. Authors also fine-tune the actor (online SFT), so some gain is not from the gate. Paper dated October 2026; NeurIPS 2026 acceptance per abstract page.
agent_relevance: A running example of VoI as a gate inside an agent loop; supports G1 (doubt only on signal).

source: Park, Im and Kwon (2026) SAG matched controls
finding: Always-on critique gets nearly the same success at far higher cost. No critic loses most of the gain. Both ambiguity signals matter, margin more.
numbers: Gated SAG 78.3 percent at 56k tokens; always-on critique plus SFT 74.2 percent at 341k tokens; ReAct plus SFT no critique 30.2 percent; critic disabled 33.0 percent. Removing entropy 77.6, removing margin 74.6. Critic calls fell 2.85 to 1.10 as success rose 71.0 to 83.0 percent.
limits: Single paper, ALFWorld ablation. Same thresholds across benchmarks, no per-task tuning claimed.
agent_relevance: Selective checking costs about 6 times fewer tokens than always checking, with a higher score.

source: Amin (2026) Bayesian Orchestration of Multi-LLM Agents
finding: LLMs act as likelihood models, beliefs are updated by Bayes rule, action is chosen to minimize expected cost, and VoI decides when to gather more information (disagreement-triggered).
numbers: Resume screening, 1,000 resumes, 5 LLMs. Costs 40,000 per missed hire, 2,500 per interview, 150 per phone screen. Total cost down 294,000 (34 percent) vs best single LLM. Demographic parity gap 22 to 5 points. Attribution: multi-LLM 51, sequential updating 43, information gathering 20 percent (sums over 100, unexplained).
limits: Single author, preprint, one task, data source unclear. Attribution does not add up. Abstract page only.
agent_relevance: Shows that asymmetric costs (270x) change the decision rule from 'most likely class'. Treat numbers as unverified.

source: Chhikara (2026) Confidence-Gated Retrieval with Matched Trajectory Replay
finding: Calibrating verbalized confidence changes which answers are committed to, but does not tell you the benefit of one more retrieval. A separate VoI estimate is needed.
numbers: 3 models x 2 datasets (HotpotQA, MuSiQue). Committed-answer accuracy up to +41 points. Overall accuracy up to +15 on HotpotQA, down to -17 on MuSiQue. Calibration map worse than raw confidence at retrieval depth 3 for all three models.
limits: Only abstract page read. Full tables not read.
agent_relevance: Negative result: confidence is not VoI. Keeps VoI out of 'is the model sure'.

source: Ding et al. (2026) Whom to Query for What
finding: LLM-based expected information gain picks survey questions, a graph network imputes missing answers and picks respondents under budget.
numbers: More than 12 percent relative gain on the CES dataset at 10 percent respondent budget. 3 real datasets. ICML 2026.
limits: Abstract page only. Other datasets and LLMs not read.
agent_relevance: EIG-based selection under a budget works for population questions, a variant of S7.

source: Li et al. (2023) Eliciting Human Preferences with Language Models (GATE)
finding: GPT-4 asks open-ended or yes/no questions to elicit user preferences. This beats user-written prompts and non-interactive baselines in most settings. No explicit information gain: the LM chooses questions by prompt.
numbers: Three domains (content recommendation, moral reasoning, email validation). Beat no elicitation in all, significant for all but email. Better than user-written prompts in 6 of 10 settings (absolute) and 7 of 10 (AUC). Yes/no generation beat user prompts in every setting. Preference entropy 0.77 bits per question on average.
limits: GPT-4-0613 only. Human participants few, power limited in moral domain. Prompts alone, no VoI calculation.
agent_relevance: Baseline: prompted question asking helps but is not optimized.

source: Piriyakulkij, Kuleshov and Ellis (2023) Active Preference Inference with LMs and probabilistic reasoning
finding: Off-the-shelf LLMs ask relevant but not informative questions. Choosing among LLM-generated yes/no questions by expected entropy reduction (an LLM-defined probabilistic model) gives better task performance with fewer turns.
numbers: Simplified web shopping with real product items; abstract states better performance with fewer interactions; exact percentages not extracted.
limits: Workshop paper. Numbers not extracted here.
agent_relevance: Same conclusion as UoT: generate with the model, rank by expected entropy in code.

source: Andukuri et al. (2024) STaR-GATE
finding: Fine-tuning a questioner by self-play, keeping conversations that raise the log-probability of a gold response, teaches it to ask better questions.
numbers: mistral-7b-instruct questioner. Responses preferred over the initial model on 72 percent of tasks after two iterations. With a weaker roleplayer 65 percent, with gemma roleplayer peak 62 percent. Fixed response model: 57 percent then back to 50 at iteration 3. 25,500 persona-task prompts. Self-oracle llama3-8b run about 65 percent after one iteration.
limits: Training, not a scaffold. Needs a stronger oracle with access to the persona. GPT-4 as judge.
agent_relevance: Score for a question = how much the gold answer becomes more likely: a VoI-like reward.

source: Grand et al. (2024) Loose LIPS sink ships (Battleship questions)
finding: Sample k questions from an LLM, run each against a hypothesis space, keep the one with highest expected information gain. Small k brings LLMs to human level, larger k beats humans.
numbers: 18 boards, 605 human questions from 40 people. Human mean EIG 1.27 bits, best human 3.61, 97 percent of human questions informative. Raw LLM questions (k=1) EIG 0.65 to 0.66, grammar 0.36. k=5 near human mean; k=10 beats human mean (p<0.001 CodeLlama-7b, p=0.01 GPT-4). 40 percent (CodeLlama) and 33 percent (GPT-4) of valid programs had EIG 0. GPT-4V gave no gain over text.
quote: questions from CodeLlama and GPT-4 averaged EIG = 0.65-0.66
limits: Needs a program-based world model. Grid game. LLMs struggle with grounding.
agent_relevance: Best-of-k questions by EIG is cheap. A third of raw model questions told you nothing; filter them by code.

source: Kobalczyk et al. (2025) Active Task Disambiguation with LLMs
finding: Treat clarifying questions as Bayesian experimental design: sample candidate solutions, choose the question with the highest information gain over them. Better than asking the LLM for the best question directly.
numbers: Code tasks HumanEval and APPS with GPT-4o-mini; zero-shot accuracy 70 percent on HumanEval and 35 percent on APPS. EIG strategies reached higher accuracy after 4 elicited requirements with fewer test cases. Gap shrinks for stronger models. Open questions beat binary ones but cost more user effort.
quote: Implicit reasoning about solutions to generate the most effective clarifying question is a difficult skill for LLMs.
limits: Percentages not extracted; read from text and figure description only.
agent_relevance: Shifting reasoning from question space to solution space is the useful move.

source: Liu et al. (2024) DeLLMa decision-making under uncertainty
finding: A decision-theory scaffold: list states, forecast them, elicit utilities, pick the max expected utility action. Beats direct, CoT and self-consistency in agriculture and stock tasks.
numbers: Up to 40 percent accuracy gain, larger as the number of actions grows. Helps GPT-4, Claude 3 and Gemini 1.5. Human agreement with elicited rankings: GPT-4 70.4 percent, Gemini 1.5 69.6, Claude 3 65.3. Cost can be halved with batch API.
limits: Stock gain is small for DeLLMa-Naive because of data volatility. No question-asking step.
agent_relevance: The expected-utility step itself can be a scaffold; EVPI sits one level above it.

source: Raiffa and Schlaifer (1961) Applied Statistical Decision Theory; Howard (1966) Information value theory
finding: Founding works for expected value of information. Not opened this session; cited by Dong et al. (2026) as the basis of VoI.
numbers: not extracted
limits: Founding numbers not read.
agent_relevance: See other angles' files for the human and theory side.

source: Claxton et al. (2002) A rational framework for decision making by NICE
finding: Health technology decisions priced with EVPI. Cited by the Wikipedia article; paper itself not opened.
numbers: not extracted
limits: Paywalled; not read.
agent_relevance: EVPI as a cap on research spending.
